A1.actual_abstract: How well can a dealer forecast the largest absolute recorded net position before a reporting horizon ends? Such forecasts motivate evaluating a monitoring input for the measured position series. We compare historical peak constructions with ridge quantile regression and local quantiles on a market maker's FX client-flow series and a weekly Treasury-dealer aggregate. The common target includes the observed issue position and uses completed training labels. First, six-record FX regression lowers matched-history pinball loss by 14.77%, while breaches rise from 360 to 376. Second, the Treasury primary deteriorates by 50.79%, with breaches rising from 28 to 54. Third, lower pinball loss often accompanies more breach occasions. The evidence is specific to the inspected records, stipulated score and source-measurement conventions.

actual_intro_paragraphs: Dealers absorb customer order imbalances while managing inventory risk and scarce balance-sheet capacity. Inventory affects optimal dealer pricing (Ho and Stoll, 1981), FX dealing (Lyons, 1995), and observed inventory adjustment in dealership markets (Hansch, Naik and Viswanathan, 1998). Treasury intermediation likewise depends on dealer capacity (Duffie et al., 2023). A forecast of the maximum recorded position magnitude over a future horizon may support monitoring of the measured position: an endpoint can return toward its starting value after an intervening large position. Translating that monitoring signal into a particular margin or financing decision requires the corresponding contractual and balance-sheet inputs.

We ask whether mature conditional estimators improve forecasts of an absolute sampled-position peak relative to simple historical constructions. Every report is evaluated against the same peak response and upper-quantile score on common issue origins. The endpoint-derived bound introduced below is a benchmark rather than a direct peak-quantile estimate. The historical alternatives use past headrooms, paths translated to the current signed position, or native peaks floored at the observed current magnitude. The conditional alternatives use ridge quantile regression, nearest-neighbor quantiles and scaled nearest-neighbor quantiles.

The matched-history FX regression comparison lowers mean loss by 14.77%, but increases breaches from 360 to 376. The original FX primary uses a different historical window and lowers loss by 12.66%. The separately declared Treasury primary deteriorates by 50.79%, with 54 rather than 28 breaches. Short-history FX regression also deteriorates at the longer horizon; a Treasury neighbor gain reverses on the sparse grid. These adverse outcomes are central findings.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it places established forecasting engines and historical constructions on a common completed-peak response with an explicit issue-known floor. Second, it controls completed-label pools and update schedules and retains the complete favorable and adverse model menu. Third, it documents how score, breach frequency, report coherence and fixed-report preferences can disagree across two financial measurement processes. The contribution is an application and model-validation benchmark using mature methods.

Section 2 locates the study in the literature. Sections 3–5 describe data, forecasts and evaluation. Sections 6–7 report FX and Treasury results. Section 8 collects exploratory robustness evidence, Section 9 discusses mechanisms and limitations, and Section 10 concludes. Detailed historical menus, geometry and supplementary diagnostics appear in the appendices.
